title: Incentivizing Crowds and Intergroup Spillovers: Evidence from the Internet Bug Bounty Program
authors: Jiali Zhou; Kai-Lung Hui; Ohchan Kwon
eligible_reason: Single common treatment date, not staggered. Python joined the Internet Bug Bounty in November 2013; Python core maintainers are treated and Java (OpenJDK) maintainers are the control group. Every DiD column (Tables 4, 5, 6, 9, 10) regresses the outcome on D = Python x post with maintainer, year and month-of-year FE on a CEM-matched sample; D switches on in 2013m11 for all 92 treated maintainers (checked in Reports.dta). Table 7 is OLS/IV of enhancement on bug reporting within Python.
design_notes: code/main analysis.do: reg y D [lg_agen nversion lg_popularity] i.naid i.y i.moy if m_sample==1 & cem_matched==1, cluster(naid). Table 4 (bug reporting, col 1 without controls, cols 2-6 with time-varying controls), Table 5 (enhancement reporting, same structure), Table 6 (commits, controls), Table 9 (interest/most-active subsamples), Table 10 (workload). Table 7: ivreg2 with bot-assisted reports as instrument. Appendix: event study with pre_12..post_18, placebo dates (May 2013, Nov 2011), entropy balancing, synthetic DiD (sdid), module-level matched analysis. Data check: min(ndate | D==1) = 201311 for all 92 treated naid; D = 0 for every Java maintainer.
data_files_note: Maintainer-month panel built from public Python/OpenJDK issue trackers and GitHub; author_code anonymizes maintainers.
screener_notes: Published PDF read (data/text/mnsc/mnsc.2024.04544.txt). Two-group single-date DiD (Python vs Java), so it fails the staggered-adoption rule; not a near miss.
